group.title: Communication
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: To communicate an idea or feeling.
wrong: His words conveyed nothing, so the message was clear.

words.meaning: To suggest something bad in an indirect way.
wrong: She insinuated it by saying it plainly and directly.

words.meaning: To mention something indirectly.
wrong: She alluded to it by explaining every detail.

words.meaning: To express what someone said using different words.
wrong: I paraphrased it by copying every word exactly.

words.meaning: To give the main points briefly.
examples: Please {summarize} the report in one page.
wrong: She summarized the book by reading every line aloud.

words.meaning: To make something easier to understand.
wrong: His answer clarified things, so we were more confused.

words.meaning: To show that something is especially important.
wrong: He emphasized the point by never mentioning it.

words.meaning: To say something again, for emphasis.
examples: Let me {reiterate}: the deadline is Friday.
wrong: She reiterated the rule by saying it for the first time.

words.meaning: To move away from the main subject while speaking.
examples: Sorry, I {digress}; back to the main point.
wrong: He digressed by staying exactly on topic.

words.meaning: Using more words than needed.
wrong: His speech was verbose, so it was very short.

words.meaning: Short and clear.
wrong: The summary was concise, so it went on for pages.

words.meaning: Expressed clearly in few words.
wrong: His answer was succinct, so it took an hour.

words.meaning: Language used to persuade, sometimes without real meaning.
examples: The speech was full of empty {rhetoric}.
wrong: Rhetoric is a type of math.

words.meaning: Informal; used in everyday conversation.
wrong: Colloquial language is used only in legal documents.

words.meaning: The way something is said that shows feelings.
wrong: Tone is the number of words in a sentence.

words.meaning: A short interesting story about a real event.
examples: She told a funny {anecdote} about her first job.
wrong: An anecdote is a long scientific report.

words.meaning: A mild word used instead of an unpleasant one.
wrong: A euphemism is a harsh word used to shock people.

words.meaning: A statement that has been said too often to be interesting.
wrong: A platitude is a fresh, original idea.

words.meaning: A statement that makes something seem less than it is.
examples: Saying it was warm is an {understatement}; it was 45 degrees.
wrong: An understatement makes something seem bigger than it is.

words.meaning: Saying the opposite of what you mean to mock someone.
wrong: Sarcasm means saying exactly what you mean, kindly.

words.meaning: A situation or use of words that is the opposite of what you expect.
examples: The {irony} is that the fire station burned down.
wrong: Irony is when everything happens just as you expect.

words.meaning: The skill of speaking or writing well and persuasively.
wrong: His eloquence meant he couldn’t express himself.

words.meaning: The act of making someone agree or do something.
examples: It took some {persuasion} to get him to come.
wrong: Persuasion means forcing someone with no words.

words.meaning: Written or spoken communication, especially serious discussion.
wrong: Discourse is silence with no communication.

words.meaning: A friendly relationship with good understanding.
examples: She has a good {rapport} with her students.
wrong: They have great rapport, so they never understand each other.

words.meaning: To say something that interrupts a speaker.
wrong: He interjected by waiting silently until the end.

words.meaning: To speak quietly and unclearly.
wrong: She mumbled, so everyone heard every word clearly.

words.meaning: To make someone feel less worried.
examples: The doctor {reassured} me that it was nothing serious.
wrong: He reassured me by making me more anxious.

words.meaning: A conversation, especially to solve a problem.
examples: Both sides agreed to open a {dialogue}.
wrong: A dialogue is a speech by one person with no reply.

words.meaning: To deal with a problem; or to speak to a group.
examples: We need to {address} this issue now.
wrong: They addressed the problem by ignoring it.

words.meaning: In a clear and effective way when speaking.
wrong: He spoke articulately, mumbling so nobody understood.

words.meaning: A movement of the hand or head that shows a meaning.
examples: He made a friendly {gesture} with his hand.
wrong: A gesture is a word you write down.

words.meaning: Movements and positions that show what you feel.
examples: His {body language} showed he was nervous.
wrong: Body language is the grammar of written English.

words.meaning: In a careful way that avoids upsetting people.
wrong: He tactfully insulted everyone in the room.

words.meaning: To listen secretly to other people’s conversation.
wrong: She eavesdropped by joining the conversation openly.

words.meaning: To tell someone a secret because you trust them.
wrong: He confided in me by keeping his secret to himself.

words.meaning: The skill of public speaking.
wrong: Oratory is the skill of writing private letters.

words.meaning: Special words used by a group that others find hard to understand.
examples: The report was full of legal {jargon}.
wrong: Jargon is simple language that everyone understands.

words.meaning: An idea or feeling a word suggests beyond its basic meaning.
wrong: A connotation is the dictionary definition only.

words.meaning: The level of formality of language.
examples: Use a formal {register} in a cover letter.
wrong: Register is the speed at which you speak.
